In this booklet, we will watch where a patch of sunlight falls on the classroom floor over three school days. You will work with the same partner each day. Together, you will check the floor at the beginning of the morning lesson and immediately after lunch. One drawing shows where the light is once. It does not show whether that position changes. Even six drawings only show the position of the light that could be seen. They do not answer every question about why it is there.

Each time you look, mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan and write the time beside it. A pencil and a ruler are provided. A ruler is useful for drawing a straight line. It does not make a fuzzy edge less fuzzy. If part of the outline is fuzzy, use a dotted line for that part instead of deciding the edge must be sharp. Two groups may mark the same edge differently. They should compare what they noticed before deciding whether either drawing needs to change.

Some days the light may not be visible. When that happens, write “no patch visible” in the space for that observation and leave the map itself unmarked. Do not draw where the patch was yesterday. Writing “no patch visible” counts as an observation. It does not count as a measurement of the patch’s position. The curtains will stay in their usual position, but the class will not control the clouds or record their thickness.

At the end, compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Write one sentence about a pattern you can support and one question that remains. You are not required to find a particular pattern. If too few patches were visible to establish a pattern, say so and explain which observations are missing. A careful account of what could not be observed is useful. A confident account of a patch nobody saw is not.

Welcome to the garden. Your assigned bed is marked with the number on your membership card, though a few of the painted numbers have faded. If you are unsure which plot is yours, the plan on the noticeboard is the most reliable guide, and please ask a steward before planting in any bed whose number you cannot read. Keep in mind, too, that the narrow strip beside the compost bins is planted collectively and is not an unclaimed bed.

That collective strip and the young fruit trees are cared for through the shared watering rota. The rota does not cover individual beds, even those belonging to gardeners who have signed up for rota shifts. If you will be away, you can make a separate watering arrangement with another gardener, but please add it to the noticeboard only after they have agreed—that way, an open request will not be mistaken for a job someone has already accepted.

When you need equipment, you will find the shed code on your membership card. Tools with blue handles belong to the shared collection; please return them to the shed before you leave the garden, even if you plan to come back later that evening. Tools without a blue handle may belong to another gardener and are not automatically shared. Whenever you leave the shed, please close the door so rain does not reach the lower shelves.

As you clear and tend your plot, weeds without seed heads can go into the green compost bay, while weeds with seed heads belong in the covered brown bin. If you are unsure whether a plant has set seed, leave it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. This is simply a sorting precaution to protect the shared compost, not a judgment on anybody's gardening.

Stewards are usually present on Saturday mornings, with the next session and any cancellations listed on the noticeboard. We are glad you are here—and please remember that we would much rather answer a small question before you plant than help move a thriving crop out of somebody else's bed.

### New in Desktop Reading Settings: Stop Image Descriptions When You Move Keyboard Focus

This desktop release introduces **Pause on Focus**, a new option in **Reading** settings that gives you more control over spoken image descriptions when navigating with a keyboard.

By default, once an image description begins speaking, it continues playing even if you move keyboard focus to another control. That remains the default behavior after updating, but you can now choose to have descriptions stop as soon as you move on.

---

#### How It Works
When you turn on **Pause on Focus** in **Reading** settings:
* **Moving focus stops playback:** Moving keyboard focus to a different control immediately stops the current image description.
* **Replaying starts from the beginning:** Moving focus back to the image will not automatically resume speech. To hear the description again from the start, use the existing **Read Description** command.
* **Your saved descriptions stay intact:** The setting does not alter the descriptions themselves. The option uses the word "pause" because stopping playback does not delete the saved description—not because playback resumes from the exact word where it stopped.

---

#### How It Works with Your Existing Description Settings
* **Automatic descriptions stay as you set them:** If you have already turned off automatic image descriptions, updating the app or enabling **Pause on Focus** will not turn them back on.
* **Works with manual descriptions, too:** Because **Pause on Focus** also stops descriptions that you trigger manually, it is still useful even if you keep automatic descriptions disabled.

---

#### Current Scope and Limitations
Keep these boundaries in mind, especially if you have more than one audio or speech source active at the same time:
* **Application speech only:** **Pause on Focus** only affects image descriptions spoken directly by the application.
* **Separate screen readers:** Speech from an external screen reader remains controlled by that screen reader, even when it is describing the same image. As a result, turning on this option will not necessarily stop all speech when focus moves.
* **Video audio:** Audio inside a video is unaffected and remains controlled by the video player.
* **Desktop only:** This option is available only in the desktop application. The mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

---

#### Reporting an Issue
If an image description continues speaking after keyboard focus has visibly moved, please let us know:
* **What to include:** Tell us the specific action you used to move focus—this is much more helpful for troubleshooting than sending the contents of the image.
* **Speech source (if known):** If you can tell whether the continuing speech came from the application or a separate screen reader, please include that detail, though you do not need to identify the source before submitting a report.

Here is a quick guide to how the new option works, how it interacts with your existing preferences, and what to expect.

---

### What It Does

When navigating with a keyboard, spoken image descriptions have always continued playing even after you move focus away from an image to another control. 

* **The Default Behavior:** Image descriptions will continue speaking when you move focus, just as before.
* **The New Option:** Enabling **Pause on Focus** stops the application's spoken description as soon as your keyboard focus leaves the image.

* **Why it’s called “Pause”:** We chose the name “pause” because stopping speech preserves the generated description in memory without deleting it. It does *not* mean speech will resume from the exact word where it stopped. 
* **Returning to the image:** Moving focus back to the image will not automatically resume playback.
* **Hearing the description again:** To listen to the description from the beginning, use the existing **Read Description** command.

* **Works with Manual Requests:** Pause on Focus also applies to descriptions you request manually. Even if automatic descriptions are disabled, you can still take advantage of this feature.

---

### Current Scope and Limitations

* **Desktop Only:** Pause on Focus is available exclusively on the desktop application. The mobile app continues to operate with its current behavior.
* **Application Speech vs. Screen Readers:** This setting controls only the audio spoken directly by our application. If you use a separate screen reader, that screen reader manages its own speech—even when reading the same image. Consequently, turning on Pause on Focus will not necessarily silence all active speech on your system.
* **Embedded Video Audio:** This feature does not affect audio within video players, which remains independently controlled by the player itself.

---

We evaluated an automated background-subtraction worksheet designed to replace manual per-sample blank entry by importing blank readings directly from the instrument log. Although eliminating manual transcription is intended to reduce entry errors that can cause discrepancies between worksheets, this comparison assessed only numerical agreement between the background-corrected fluorescence values produced by the two methods. Because the experiment did not include certified reference material, the results do not evaluate analytical accuracy against a known true concentration.

In a single session, 24 aliquots drawn from eight prepared solutions (three aliquots per solution) were measured in a fixed order by solution number. Each aliquot was measured only once, and both worksheets processed the identical set of raw instrument readings; consequently, the dataset contains no independent repeats of the instrument signal despite including three aliquots per prepared solution. A single operator, who was aware that the comparison examined data entry, completed and checked the manual worksheet before the imported worksheet was generated and therefore could not see the imported results while entering the manual values.

In the initial comparison, the reported background-corrected values agreed to the instrument's displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots. The remaining three discrepancies all occurred in the final solution. Inspection of the saved instrument log showed that a single blank entry—0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank assigned to those rows in the log—had been copied across all three rows for that solution in the manual worksheet, making the resulting manual corrected values 0.2 fluorescence units lower than the imported values. In a separate post-hoc check performed after the initial comparison, replacing that copied manual entry with the logged blank brought the corrected values for all 24 aliquots into agreement at the instrument's displayed precision.

First, the complete agreement across all 24 aliquots after correcting the single manual entry provides useful evidence that the import worksheet applied the intended background subtraction to these inputs; however, this result is limited to the instrument's displayed precision and does not establish agreement at higher precision or guarantee correct blank assignment in future instrument logs. Moreover, because only one operator participated and knew the evaluation focused on data entry, the observed error cannot be treated as an estimate of a routine operator error rate.

# Evaluation of Automated Log Import versus Manual Entry for Fluorescence Background Subtraction

### Objective and Scope
This evaluation compared two methods for background subtraction in fluorescence data processing:
1. **Manual Worksheet:** The existing workflow requiring the operator to transcribe blank readings individually for each sample.
2. **Imported Worksheet:** A proposed workflow that automatically imports blank readings directly from the instrument log to eliminate manual transcription.

The objective was to evaluate agreement between corrected values produced by each worksheet when processing identical instrument readings. This assessment is limited strictly to relative agreement between the two calculation workflows; it does not assess analytical accuracy against an absolute concentration, as certified reference materials were not evaluated.

---

### Experimental Design and Data Collection
* **Sample Structure:** Twenty-four aliquots representing eight prepared solutions (three aliquots per solution) were measured in a single analytical session.
* **Measurement Sequence:** Aliquots were measured in a fixed sequence governed by solution number. Each aliquot was measured once without duplicate instrument acquisitions; thus, the dataset does not provide independent replicates of the instrument signal.
* **Blinding and Workflow Controls:** To prevent bias during data entry, the manual worksheet was fully populated and checked before the imported worksheet was generated. The operator had no access to the imported results while entering manual data.

---

### Initial Results and Discrepancy Investigation
* **Initial Agreement:** Corrected values from the two worksheets agreed within the instrument's displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots.
* **Discrepancy Identification:** The three discordant values occurred exclusively in the final solution. In the manual worksheet, a single blank reading had been copied across the three corresponding sample rows.
* **Root-Cause Analysis:** Cross-referencing the saved instrument log revealed that the manually entered blank was 0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank value logged for those rows. Consequently, the manual corrected values were 0.2 units lower than the imported values.
* **Post-Investigation Resolution:** Substituting the logged blank value into the manual worksheet brought all 24 corrected values into complete agreement at the displayed precision. ## Pilot Findings: Grate Cover Evaluation

### 1. Study Design and Measurement Protocol
The pilot examined whether installing a different grate cover would reduce the time water remained above the pavement following rain. Observations covered six drains across two streets over eight storms—four storms before the cover change and four storms afterward—yielding a complete set of 48 drain-storm observations (12 per street in each period). 

Cover allocation was non-random: crews replaced the covers on the three lower-street drains because that street had generated more prior complaints, while the three upper-street drains retained their existing covers. On the day the covers were changed, crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains.

During each storm, a fixed camera at each drain recorded the number of minutes water remained visible above a painted reference line. A recorded duration of zero indicates only that water did not rise above the reference line, not an absence of runoff. Staff reported that all 48 recordings were scorable, establishing the practical feasibility of capturing the camera-based measure for these eight storms, though inter-scorer reliability (whether different raters assign identical durations) has not been tested.

### 2. Observed Measurements and Scope Limitations
Across both streets, camera records showed shorter mean durations of water above the reference line during the four storms following the intervention:

| Location | Condition | Pre-Change Mean Duration (12 observations) | Post-Change Mean Duration (12 observations) | Observed Change |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Lower Street (3 drains)** | Grate covers replaced; leaves cleared | 18 minutes | 10 minutes | −8 minutes |
| **Upper Street (3 drains)** | Existing covers retained; leaves cleared | 9 minutes | 7 minutes | −2 minutes |

These measurements reflect only the duration of visible water above the painted reference line and must be distinguished from unmeasured outcomes and parameters:
* **Drainage capacity:** Physical drainage capacity was not directly measured.
* **Peak water depth:** Peak depth was not extracted from the camera images, even though changes in peak depth could be consequential without a corresponding change in duration above the reference line.
* **Property impacts:** Flooded properties and property damage were not observed or measured.
* **Local precipitation and debris:** Neither street had a local rain gauge, no within-storm rainfall intensity data were collected, and the volume of leaves removed during the maintenance clearing was not recorded.

### 3. Unresolved Explanatory Factors
Although the mean duration fell more on the lower street (8 minutes) than on the upper street (2 minutes), this comparison does not isolate a causal effect of the replacement grate covers. Several confounding factors remain unresolved:
* **Non-random selection:** The lower street was selected because of higher complaint volume and began with a higher baseline duration (18 minutes versus 9 minutes).

---

## 2. Observed Measurements
Ponding duration was monitored using fixed cameras positioned at each drain during each storm event. All 48 planned drain-storm observations (six drains across eight storms) were recorded and available for analysis.

* **Metric Definition:** The metric recorded was the number of minutes surface water remained above a painted pavement reference line. A recorded duration of zero indicates that water did not rise above the reference line; it does not indicate an absence of runoff reaching the drain.
* **Scoring Feasibility:** Field and analysis staff confirmed that all 48 recordings could be scored.
* **Duration Trends:**
  * **Lower Street (Replacement Covers):** The mean recorded ponding duration across 12 observations dropped from 18 minutes before the change to 10 minutes afterward (an 8-minute decrease).
  * **Upper Street (Retained Covers):** The mean recorded ponding duration across 12 observations dropped from 9 minutes before the change to 7 minutes afterward (a 2-minute decrease).
  * **Observed Comparison:** Both sets of drains showed shorter ponding durations in the second observation period, with the lower street exhibiting a greater net reduction.

---

## 3. Boundaries of the Measurement
To avoid misinterpreting the camera-based observations, the following distinctions must be maintained:

* **Ponding Duration vs. Drainage Capacity:** A decline in minutes above the painted reference line cannot be treated as a direct measurement of increased hydraulic intake or drainage conveyance capacity, neither of which was measured.

* **Surface Metrics vs. Property Impact:** The pilot gathered no observations regarding property damage or structural flooding. Changes in recorded ponding duration cannot be equated to reductions in flooded properties.

---

While the lower street experienced a greater reduction in ponding duration, this comparison alone does not isolate a grate cover effect due to several unmeasured and concurrent variables:

* **Scorer Reliability:** It has not yet been evaluated whether independent scorers applying the criteria to the same video footage arrive at identical duration values.
* **Future Study Design:**

# Research Summary: Spoken Location Cues When Returning from a Note to a Table

When a user closes a note, our existing table view returns keyboard focus to the cell they left. Does returning focus return the user's attention to the right place? To find out whether an explicit audio landmark helps, we built a prototype version that speaks the current row label when the note closes and compared it against the existing silent focus return.

### How We Tested
Twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with the spoken cue and four tasks with the existing version. We timed only the return journey: the clock started when the participant closed the note and stopped when they activated the requested table entry. Reading the note itself sat outside the timed window.

To keep version order and table familiarity from lining up completely, six participants used the cue version first and six used the existing version first. We used different tables for the two four-task sets and reversed which table paired with which version for half of each order group. 

Did the counterbalancing eliminate practice effects? No. It prevented version and practice from overlapping completely, but it could not stop a participant from working out a search strategy during their first four tasks and carrying that habit into the second set. Our scope had two other boundaries: every participant was an experienced screen-reader user, and every prototype table fit on a single screen. We do not know how less experienced users would respond or how the cue behaves on large tables.

### What the Timings Show—and What They Do Not
For each participant, we calculated a mean completion time in each condition. Across the twelve participants, the median of those participant-level means was **38 seconds** with the cue and **41 seconds** without it. 

What does that three-second gap actually represent? It is the difference between two group medians, not the median of twelve within-person differences. Looking within individuals at the recorded precision, seven participants had a lower personal mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means. We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test, so these timings describe our sample rather than establish a reliable speed advantage.

### What Participants Reported
In closing interviews, nine of the twelve participants said the cue helped them feel oriented. Saying a cue feels orienting in an interview is self-reported perception, not measured navigation performance, and even among those nine users the cue carried a cost: four of them described moments when the row announcement interrupted speech they were still listening to.

The remaining three participants reported no orientation benefit. None of them asked us to remove the cue from the prototype, but should we read silence as support for turning it on by default? No. Not asking to remove a prototype feature is not the same as wanting it enabled by default, and we did not ask participants to choose a default setting.

### Implications for the Next Iteration
These observations make an orientation benefit plausible for some experienced users on short tables, while exposing a direct tradeoff: added speech competes with ongoing speech. Even if future testing shows a reliable time savings, that speech collision remains a design problem we have to solve.

One candidate for the next iteration is making the spoken cue interruptible. Would an interruptible cue preserve the orientation cue without stepping on active audio? That requires its own test. We did not build or evaluate interruptible behavior in this study, so the current timings and interview responses must not be cited as evidence for it.

# Classroom Materials Evaluation: Side-by-Side vs. Reference-Page Worksheet Diagrams

### Overview of the Comparison
This evaluation examined two versions of a single-lesson worksheet asking pupils to explain why the same amount of water appears different in a tall vessel versus a wide vessel. Both versions used identical question wording, question order, and diagrams, differing only in layout:
* **Version A (Side-by-Side Layout):** Placed the relevant diagram directly beside each question.
* **Version B (Reference-Page Layout):** Grouped the same diagrams together on a separate reference page.

Four classes completed the worksheets during a single lesson—two classes using Version A and two using Version B. Teachers selected which version their class would use before seeing any pupil responses. All teachers worked from the same written instructions, though they were free to answer pupil questions during the lesson.

---

### Sample and Scoring Procedure
Only returned worksheets were included in the analysis:
* **Version A:** 52 worksheets returned (6 additional assigned pupils were absent).
* **Version B:** 49 worksheets returned (5 additional assigned pupils were absent).

To prevent layout bias during marking, responses to the final explanation question were transcribed so the scorer could not see which worksheet version a pupil had used. Responses were scored on a two-point scale:
* **1 point** for stating that the amount of water remained unchanged.
* **1 point** for explaining that the shape of the vessel changed the water level.

To check the scoring procedure, a second scorer independently marked 10 transcribed answers. The two scorers agreed on 9 of the 10 responses and resolved the 10th through discussion before final totals were compiled. While this small check helps document how the scoring rule worked in practice, it is not a complete reliability study.

---

### Findings on the Final Explanation Question

| Score on Final Question | Version A: Side-by-Side ($n = 52$) | Version B: Reference Page ($n = 49$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **2 points** (Both criteria met) | 31 worksheets | 27 worksheets |
| **1 point** (One criterion met) | 15 worksheets | 16 worksheets |
| **0 points** (Neither criterion met) | 6 worksheets | 6 worksheets |

In these four classes, the side-by-side layout (Version A) was associated with a somewhat higher proportion of fully credited (2-point) answers than the reference-page layout (Version B), while equal numbers of worksheets in both groups received zero points.

---

### Scope and Limitations of the Evaluation
When interpreting these results for classroom practice, several constraints of the completed evaluation apply:
* **Uncontrolled classroom and assignment factors:** Because teachers chose which version their classes used and unrecorded teacher–pupil Q&A took place during the lesson, neither pupil assignment nor teacher assistance was controlled. The evaluation cannot separate the effect of worksheet layout from existing class differences or in-lesson support.
* **No baseline measure:** No prior task was scored, so the two groups' starting knowledge before the lesson is unknown.
* **Single-question scope:** The scores reflect written responses to one explanation question rather than a comprehensive measure of pupils' general understanding of volume.
* **No pupil preference data:** Pupils were not asked which layout they preferred, so the evaluation provides no evidence on pupil preference.

Overall, this completed evaluation offers a concrete comparison of the returned responses across the four participating classes and clarifies the classroom and baseline records a more controlled evaluation would need to capture.

Approve the purchase and installation of two automatic flood-warning signs for the underpass (estimated at 18,000 units of local currency, excluding annual maintenance), **subject to three explicit conditions**:

The purchase should not be treated as ready for unconditional approval while staffing and backup closure arrangements remain unresolved.

---

### Rationale

#### 1. Addressing Delayed Warnings vs. Resolving Flooding
The underpass sometimes floods before maintenance crews can arrive to close the road. Automatic signs address this specific gap by providing earlier warning when water levels cross a set sensor threshold.

However, **public warning is not physical protection**. Installing signs completes a warning project, not the flood-mitigation work:
* **Warning signs (18,000 units initial estimate)** alert approaching drivers to water in the roadway but do nothing to keep water out.
* **Drainage pipe replacement (140,000 units initial estimate)** addresses the underlying drainage capacity and still requires design work.

Neither cost estimate includes annual maintenance, and there is no agreed estimate of how much either option would reduce injuries or vehicle damage. Consequently, the warning signs must be evaluated on their merits as a response to delayed road closures—not as a cheaper substitute for pipe replacement or a way to achieve the same outcome.

Automated warning equipment reduces risk from delayed crew arrival, and it should not be rejected simply because it cannot prevent every unsafe entry. At the same time, its operational limits explain why approval must be conditional:
* **Power and Sensor Failures:** Because sensors can fail and electronic signs require power, an unlit sign does not guarantee a clear road; it may mean the system is offline. This makes monthly sensor inspections and a manual closure fallback essential.
* **Driver Compliance:** The proposal includes a permanent static notice advising drivers that water may be present even when the electronic sign is off. While necessary, neither the permanent notice nor the active signs can prevent drivers from overlooking or disregarding warnings.

# Classroom Handout: Telescoping Series of Successive Differences

### Theorem
Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0$. For each integer $n \ge 1$, define
$$d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}.$$
Then:
1. Every term $d_n$ is nonnegative ($d_n \ge 0$).
2. The infinite series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to $a_1$.
3. For every integer $N \ge 1$, the tail of the series after $N$ terms converges and satisfies
   $$\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}.$$
4. In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an integer $N \ge 1$ such that
   $$\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n < \varepsilon.$$

---

### Proof

#### Step 1: Nonnegativity of $d_n$
By assumption, the sequence $(a_n)$ is nonincreasing, which means
$$a_1 \ge a_2 \ge a_3 \ge \cdots \ge a_n \ge a_{n+1} \ge \cdots.$$
Subtracting $a_{n+1}$ from both sides of the inequality $a_n \ge a_{n+1}$ gives
$$d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0 \quad \text{for every } n \ge 1.$$

*Remark on edge cases:* Strict decrease ($a_n > a_{n+1}$) is not required. Whenever two consecutive terms are equal ($a_n = a_{n+1}$), the corresponding difference is simply $d_n = 0$, which still satisfies $d_n \ge 0$ and contributes $0$ to any sum. In the extreme case where $a_1 = 0$, nonnegativity and monotonicity ($0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$) force $a_n = 0$ and $d_n = 0$ for all $n \ge 1$, and all identities below still hold with both sides equal to $0$.

---

#### Step 2: Convergence of the Series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ to $a_1$
By definition, an infinite series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to a value $S$ if and only if its sequence of finite partial sums
$$S_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n$$
converges to $S$ as $N \to \infty$. Because $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}$, we can evaluate $S_N$ directly without appealing to any external convergence test.

For any integer $N \ge 1$, write out the partial sum $S_N$:
$$S_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n = (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + (a_3 - a_4) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1}).$$
This is a **telescoping sum**: each subtracted term $-a_k$ (for $2 \le k \le N$) is immediately canceled by the $+a_k$ in the next parenthesis:
$$S_N = a_1 + (-a_2 + a_2) + (-a_3 + a_3) + \cdots + (-a_N + a_N) - a_{N+1} = a_1 - a_{N+1}.$$

Now take the limit as $N \to \infty$. Since $\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0$, the shifted sequence $(a_{N+1})$ also satisfies $\lim_{N \to \infty} a_{N+1} = 0$. Because $a_1$ does not depend on $N$, the limit law for differences yields
$$\lim_{N \to \infty} S_N = \lim_{N \to \infty} (a_1 - a_{N+1}) = a_1 - \lim_{N \to \infty} a_{N+1} = a_1 - 0 = a_1.$$
Since the partial sums $S_N$ converge to $a_1$, the infinite series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges and equals $a_1$.

---

#### Step 3: Evaluating the Tail After $N$ Terms
Fix an integer $N \ge 1$. The **tail** of the series after $N$ terms is the infinite series $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n$. By definition, this tail is the limit as $M \to \infty$ of the finite sums from $n = N+1$ to $n = M$ (where $M > N$).

Writing out the finite sum for any integer $M > N$, we see the same telescoping cancellation starting at $a_{N+1}$ and ending at $a_{M+1}$:
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n = (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + (a_{N+2} - a_{N+3}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1}) = a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.$$
Here every intermediate term $a_{N+2}, a_{N+3}, \dots, a_M$ cancels in pairs, leaving only the first term $a_{N+1}$ and the last term $-a_{M+1}$.

With $N$ held fixed, $a_{N+1}$ is a constant as $M$ varies. Taking the limit as $M \to \infty$ and using $\lim_{M \to \infty} a_{M+1} = 0$, we obtain
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = \lim_{M \to \infty} \sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n = \lim_{M \to \infty} (a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}) = a_{N+1} - \lim_{M \to \infty} a_{M+1} = a_{N+1} - 0 = a_{N+1}.$$

---

#### Step 4: Making the Tail Smaller Than $\varepsilon$
Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given. We wish to find an integer $N \ge 1$ such that $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n < \varepsilon$.

By Step 3, the tail after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$, so it suffices to find $N \ge 1$ such that $a_{N+1} < \varepsilon$.
1. Because $\lim_{k \to \infty} a_k = 0$ and $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k$, the definition of sequence convergence guarantees that there exists an integer $K$ such that
   $$a_k = |a_k - 0| < \varepsilon \quad \text{whenever } k \ge K.$$
2. Set $N = \max(1, K)$. Taking the maximum with $1$ ensures that $N \ge 1$ is a valid positive integer, while also ensuring $N \ge K$.
3. Because $N \ge K$, the index $k = N + 1$ satisfies $N + 1 > N \ge K$, so $a_{N+1} < \varepsilon$.

Combining this inequality with the tail formula from Step 3 gives
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon,$$
which completes the proof. $\blacksquare$

\]
Then every $d_n$ is nonnegative, the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to $a_1$, and for every integer $N \ge 1$ its tail after $N$ terms satisfies

\]
In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists an integer $N \ge 1$ such that $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n < \varepsilon$.

**Proof.** Because $(a_n)$ is nonincreasing, $a_n \ge a_{n+1}$ for every integer $n \ge 1$. Subtracting $a_{n+1}$ from both sides gives

\]
If consecutive terms are equal ($a_n = a_{n+1}$), then $d_n = 0$, so the argument does not require $(a_n)$ to be strictly decreasing. To show that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to $a_1$, we evaluate its partial sums directly from the definition of series convergence. &= \sum_{n=1}^{N} (a_n - a_{n+1}) \\

&= \lim_{N \to \infty} (a_1 - a_{N+1}) \\
&= a_1 - \lim_{N \to \infty} a_{N+1} \\

\end{aligned}
\]

Finally, let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $\lim_{k \to \infty} a_k = 0$ and each $a_k \ge 0$, the definition of convergence provides an integer $K \ge 1$ such that

# Classroom Handout: Telescoping Series and Tail Bounds

---

### **Overview & Definitions**

In this handout, we study an infinite series whose terms are successive differences of a sequence. 

Recall that:
1. An **infinite series** $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges to a sum $S$ if and only if its sequence of **finite partial sums**, 
   $$S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N d_n = d_1 + d_2 + \cdots + d_N,$$
   converges to $S$ as $N \to \infty$ (that is, $\lim_{N \to \infty} S_N = S$).
2. The **tail of the series after $N$ terms**, denoted $R_N$, is the series formed by all remaining terms past index $N$:
   $$R_N = \sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = \lim_{M \to \infty} \sum_{n=N+1}^M d_n.$$

We will evaluate both the total sum and the tail directly using **elementary telescoping cancellation** and basic limit properties, without relying on black-box convergence tests.

---

### **Theorem (Convergence and Exact Tail of Difference Series)**

> Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be a real sequence satisfying:
> 1. **Nonnegativity:** $a_n \ge 0$ for all $n \ge 1$.
> 2. **Nonincreasing:** $a_1 \ge a_2 \ge a_3 \ge \cdots$ (that is, $a_n \ge a_{n+1}$ for all $n \ge 1$).
> 3. **Zero limit:** $\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0$.
>
> Define the consecutive differences by $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}$ for each $n \ge 1$.
>
> Then:
> - Every term $d_n$ is nonnegative ($d_n \ge 0$).
> - The series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges, and its sum is exactly $a_1$:
>   $$\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n = a_1.$$
> - For every integer $N \ge 1$, the tail after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$:
>   $$\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1}.$$
> - In particular, for every tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an index $N \ge 1$ such that the tail is strictly less than $\varepsilon$.

---

### **Detailed Step-by-Step Proof**

#### **Step 1: Sign of the terms $d_n$**
Because the sequence $(a_n)$ is nonincreasing, each term is at least as large as the next:
$$a_n \ge a_{n+1} \implies a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0.$$
Therefore, $d_n \ge 0$ for every $n \ge 1$. 

*(Note: We only require $a_n \ge a_{n+1}$, not strict inequality. If $a_n = a_{n+1}$, then $d_n = 0$, which is completely valid.)*

---

#### **Step 2: Telescoping the finite partial sums $S_N$**
Consider the $N$-th partial sum $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N d_n$. Writing each difference explicitly:
$$S_N = (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + (a_3 - a_4) + \cdots + (a_{N-1} - a_N) + (a_N - a_{N+1}).$$

Notice how neighboring terms cancel in pairs:
- $-a_2$ from the first term cancels $+a_2$ from the second;
- $-a_3$ from the second term cancels $+a_3$ from the third;
- and so on, continuing through $-a_N$ canceling $+a_N$.

Every intermediate term vanishes, leaving only the very first component $a_1$ and the final subtracted component $a_{N+1}$:
$$S_N = a_1 - a_{N+1}.$$

---

#### **Step 3: Convergence of the infinite series from first principles**
By definition, the infinite sum is the limit of the partial sums $S_N$ as $N \to \infty$:
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n = \lim_{N \to \infty} S_N = \lim_{N \to \infty} (a_1 - a_{N+1}).$$

Because $a_1$ is a constant and we are given that $\lim_{k \to \infty} a_k = 0$ (so $\lim_{N \to \infty} a_{N+1} = 0$), the basic limit laws give:
$$\lim_{N \to \infty} (a_1 - a_{N+1}) = a_1 - \lim_{N \to \infty} a_{N+1} = a_1 - 0 = a_1.$$

The sequence of partial sums converges to $a_1$. Thus, by definition, the series converges and:
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n = a_1.$$

---

#### **Step 4: Evaluating the tail after $N$ terms**
Fix an integer $N \ge 1$. The tail after $N$ terms is the infinite series starting at index $N+1$:
$$R_N = \sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n.$$

To evaluate this from definition, take any integer $M > N$ and write the finite sum from index $N+1$ up to $M$:
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^M d_n = (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + (a_{N+2} - a_{N+3}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1}).$$

Just as in Step 2, this finite sum telescopes completely. All intermediate terms from $a_{N+2}$ through $a_M$ cancel, leaving:
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^M d_n = a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.$$

Now keep $N$ fixed and let the upper index $M \to \infty$. Since $a_{M+1} \to 0$ as $M \to \infty$, we obtain:
$$R_N = \sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = \lim_{M \to \infty} (a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}) = a_{N+1} - \lim_{M \to \infty} a_{M+1} = a_{N+1} - 0 = a_{N+1}.$$

*(Consistency check: Subtracting the partial sum from the total sum gives $a_1 - S_N = a_1 - (a_1 - a_{N+1}) = a_{N+1}$, perfectly matching our direct calculation.)*

Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be any target error tolerance.

Since $(a_k)_{k \ge 1}$ converges to $0$, the definition of a sequence limit guarantees that there is an integer $K$ such that:
$$|a_k - 0| < \varepsilon \quad \text{for all } k \ge K.$$
Because $a_k \ge 0$, this simply means $0 \le a_k < \varepsilon$ whenever $k \ge K$.

Now choose:
$$N = \max(1, K).$$

- Because $N \ge 1$, $N$ is a valid index for a partial sum.
- Because $N \ge K$, the index of the next term satisfies $N + 1 > K$.
- Consequently, $a_{N+1} < \varepsilon$.

Since the tail after $N$ terms is exactly $a_{N+1}$, we have:
$$\text{Tail} = \sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon.$$

### **Remarks on Assumptions and Edge Cases**

1. **What if $a_1 = 0$?**  
   If $a_1 = 0$, the conditions $0 \le a_n \le a_1$ force $a_n = 0$ for every $n \ge 1$. Then $d_n = 0 - 0 = 0$ for all $n$. Every finite sum is $0 - 0 = 0$, the infinite sum converges to $a_1 = 0$, and every tail is $a_{N+1} = 0 < \varepsilon$. The identities hold seamlessly.

2. **Weak versus strict decrease:**  
   The theorem does not require strict decrease ($a_n > a_{n+1}$). If consecutive terms are equal ($a_n = a_{n+1}$), then $d_n = 0$. Adding zero terms neither disrupts telescoping cancellation nor affects the value of limits.

**Claim.** Let $(a_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers that is nonincreasing and satisfies $\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0$. For each $n \ge 1$, define $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}$. Then every $d_n$ is nonnegative, the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges to $a_1$, and for every integer $N \ge 1$, the tail after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$:
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists an integer $N \ge 1$ such that this tail is strictly less than $\epsilon$.

**Proof.**
Because the sequence $(a_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ is nonincreasing, $a_n \ge a_{n+1}$ for every $n \ge 1$. Subtracting $a_{n+1}$ gives
\[
d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0,
\]
so each term $d_n$ is nonnegative.

To establish convergence of the series, consider the $N$-th partial sum $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N d_n$ for an integer $N \ge 1$. Expanding the sum displays the telescoping cancellation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N &= (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + (a_3 - a_4) + \dots + (a_N - a_{N+1}) \\
&= a_1 - a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every intermediate term $a_2, a_3, \dots, a_N$ appears twice with opposite signs—first with a minus sign in one bracket, then with a plus sign in the next—leaving only the initial term $a_1$ and the subtracted boundary term $a_{N+1}$.

By definition, the infinite series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges if the sequence of partial sums $(S_N)_{N=1}^\infty$ converges to a finite limit. Because $\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0$, the shifted term $a_{N+1}$ also converges to zero as $N \to \infty$. Taking the limit of both sides gives
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n = \lim_{N \to \infty} S_N = \lim_{N \to \infty} (a_1 - a_{N+1}) = a_1 - 0 = a_1.
\]

Now fix an integer $N \ge 1$ and consider the tail of the series after $N$ terms. For any integer $M > N$, the finite sum from $n = N+1$ to $M$ telescopes in the same way:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^M d_n &= (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + (a_{N+2} - a_{N+3}) + \dots + (a_M - a_{M+1}) \\
&= a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Holding $N$ fixed and letting $M \to \infty$, the term $a_{M+1}$ tends to zero. Therefore,
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = \lim_{M \to \infty} \sum_{n=N+1}^M d_n = \lim_{M \to \infty} (a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}) = a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, let $\epsilon > 0$. Because $\lim_{k \to \infty} a_k = 0$ and every $a_k \ge 0$, there is an index $K \ge 1$ such that $a_k < \epsilon$ whenever $k \ge K$. Setting $N = K$, we have $N + 1 > K$, which implies $a_{N+1} < \epsilon$. Applying the tail identity yields
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1} < \epsilon.
\]

$$E[(X - c)^2] = E[(X - M)^2] + 2E[(X - M)(M - c)] + E[(M - c)^2].$$

2. **Positive-probability cells ($p_j > 0$).** By definition of conditional expectation on $G_j$,
   $$E[X \mid G_j] = \frac{1}{p_j} \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\}) X(\omega) = \mu_j.$$

   $$E[X - M \mid G_j] = E[X \mid G_j] - \mu_j = \mu_j - \mu_j = 0.$$

Substituting $E[(X - M)(M - c)] = 0$ into the expanded expectation yields
$$E[(X - c)^2] = E[(X - M)^2] + E[(M - c)^2].$$

# Teaching Note: Decomposition of Mean Squared Error by Batch Means

**Topic:** Finite-Space Derivation of the Batch-Mean Variance Identity  
**Course Context:** Laboratory Statistics & Quality Control  

---

### 1. Statement of the Claim

Let $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ be a finite probability space. Suppose:
- $X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable representing an experimental or instrument reading.
- $G_1, G_2, \dots, G_m$ is a partition of $\Omega$ into disjoint batch cells (such that $\Omega = \bigcup_{j=1}^m G_j$ and $G_j \cap G_k = \emptyset$ for $j \neq k$).
- For each cell $j \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, let $p_j = P(G_j) = \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})$.
- For cells with $p_j > 0$, define the batch mean:
  $$\mu_j = \frac{1}{p_j} \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\}) X(\omega)$$
  For cells with $p_j = 0$, set $\mu_j = 0$.
- Define the cell-mean random variable $M: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ piecewise by:
  $$M(\omega) = \mu_j \quad \text{for } \omega \in G_j$$
  (equivalently, $M = \sum_{j=1}^m \mu_j \mathbf{1}_{G_j}$).

Then for every real constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$:
$$\mathbb{E}[(X - c)^2] = \mathbb{E}[(X - M)^2] + \mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2]$$

**Consequence:** For every real constant $c$,
$$\mathbb{E}[(X - c)^2] \ge \mathbb{E}[(X - M)^2]$$
with equality if and only if $M = c$ with probability one (almost surely with respect to $P$).

---

### 2. Pedagogical Remark: The Independence Flaw in the Draft Proof

The draft proof attempted to argue that $\mathbb{E}[(X - M)(M - c)] = 0$ by asserting that the residual $X - M$ is *statistically independent* of $M$ because its conditional expectation given each cell is zero.

> **Caution for Students:** Conditional mean zero does **not** imply statistical independence.
>
> 1. **Independence vs. Orthogonality:** Statistical independence between random variables $Y$ and $Z$ requires that the joint distribution factorizes: $P(Y \in A, Z \in B) = P(Y \in A) P(Z \in B)$ for all sets $A, B$. The condition $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z] = 0$ implies only that $Y$ is *orthogonal* to every function $h(Z)$ in $L^2$ (i.e., $\mathbb{E}[Y h(Z)] = 0$), which includes uncorrelatedness.
> 2. **Physical Counterexample in the Lab:** In real analytical chemistry and testing data, the residual noise $X - M$ often exhibits *heteroscedasticity*: batches with larger baseline values or distinct experimental runs may exhibit larger measurement variances ($\operatorname{Var}(X \mid G_j)$ depends on $j$). In that case, $|X - M|$ correlates with $M$, disproving independence even though the conditional bias $\mathbb{E}[X - M \mid G_j]$ is strictly zero everywhere.

We do **not** need independence. The result requires only the cellwise-constant property of $M$ and the definition of conditional expectation on finite partitions.

---

### 3. Repaired and Complete Proof

Because $\Omega$ is finite, all expectations and probabilities are finite sums:
$$\mathbb{E}[Z] = \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} P(\{\omega\}) Z(\omega)$$

#### Step 1: Algebraic Pointwise Decomposition
Fix any constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$. For every outcome $\omega \in \Omega$, add and subtract $M(\omega)$:
$$X(\omega) - c = [X(\omega) - M(\omega)] + [M(\omega) - c]$$

Squaring both sides yields the pointwise identity:
$$(X(\omega) - c)^2 = (X(\omega) - M(\omega))^2 + 2(X(\omega) - M(\omega))(M(\omega) - c) + (M(\omega) - c)^2$$

Taking mathematical expectations of both sides using linearity:
$$\mathbb{E}[(X - c)^2] = \mathbb{E}[(X - M)^2] + 2\,\mathbb{E}[(X - M)(M - c)] + \mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2] \tag{1}$$

The target decomposition holds if and only if the cross-term vanishes:
$$\mathbb{E}[(X - M)(M - c)] = 0$$

---

#### Step 2: Evaluation of the Cross-Term via Cell Partitioning
Because $\{G_1, \dots, G_m\}$ partitions $\Omega$, the sum over all $\omega \in \Omega$ decomposes into the sum over the individual cells:
$$\mathbb{E}[(X - M)(M - c)] = \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\}) (X(\omega) - M(\omega))(M(\omega) - c)$$

Recall that by definition, $M(\omega) = \mu_j$ for all $\omega \in G_j$. Hence, the factor $(M(\omega) - c) = (\mu_j - c)$ is **constant** on $G_j$ and can be factored outside the inner summation:
$$\mathbb{E}[(X - M)(M - c)] = \sum_{j=1}^m (\mu_j - c) \underbrace{\left[ \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\}) (X(\omega) - \mu_j) \right]}_{S_j} \tag{2}$$

We evaluate the inner bracket $S_j = \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\}) X(\omega) - \mu_j \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})$ for each cell:

1. **Positive-probability cells ($p_j > 0$):**  
   Here $P(G_j) = \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\}) = p_j$. By definition of $\mu_j$:
   $$p_j \mu_j = \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\}) X(\omega)$$
   Substituting this into $S_j$:
   $$S_j = \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\}) X(\omega) - \mu_j p_j = p_j \mu_j - p_j \mu_j = 0$$
   *(In conditional expectation notation: $\mathbb{E}[X - \mu_j \mid G_j] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid G_j] - \mu_j = \mu_j - \mu_j = 0$, so $S_j = p_j \mathbb{E}[X - M \mid G_j] = 0$.)*

2. **Zero-probability cells ($p_j = 0$):**  
   If $P(G_j) = 0$, then because probabilities are non-negative and $P(G_j) = \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})$, every individual element $\omega \in G_j$ must satisfy:
   $$P(\{\omega\}) = 0$$
   Consequently, every term in the sum is zero:
   $$S_j = \sum_{\omega \in G_j} 0 \cdot (X(\omega) - 0) = 0$$
   The cell contributes zero regardless of the numerical convention assigned to $\mu_j$.

Since $S_j = 0$ for every $j \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, each term in the sum (2) vanishes:
$$\mathbb{E}[(X - M)(M - c)] = \sum_{j=1}^m (\mu_j - c) \cdot 0 = 0$$

Substituting this back into (1) completes the identity:
$$\mathbb{E}[(X - c)^2] = \mathbb{E}[(X - M)^2] + \mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2] \tag{3}$$

---

#### Step 3: Derivation of the Minimizing Bound and Equality Condition
Because squared real numbers are always non-negative:
$$(M(\omega) - c)^2 \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } \omega \in \Omega \implies \mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2] \ge 0$$
Applying this to (3) gives:
$$\mathbb{E}[(X - c)^2] \ge \mathbb{E}[(X - M)^2]$$

Equality holds if and only if:
$$\mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2] = 0$$

Expanding the expectation across the partition cells:
$$\mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2] = \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\}) (\mu_j - c)^2 = \sum_{j=1}^m p_j (\mu_j - c)^2 = 0$$

Since $p_j \ge 0$ and $(\mu_j - c)^2 \ge 0$ for all $j$, a sum of non-negative terms is zero if and only if each individual summand is zero:
$$p_j (\mu_j - c)^2 = 0 \quad \text{for every } j \in \{1, \dots, m\}$$

- For any cell where $p_j > 0$, we must have $(\mu_j - c)^2 = 0 \iff \mu_j = c$.
- For any cell where $p_j = 0$, the condition $0 \cdot (\mu_j - c)^2 = 0$ holds trivially for any value of $\mu_j$.

Therefore, $\mu_j = c$ for all cells with $p_j > 0$. The set of outcomes where $M(\omega) \neq c$ is contained within the union of zero-probability cells:
$$\{\omega \in \Omega : M(\omega) \neq c\} \subseteq \bigcup_{j : p_j = 0} G_j$$

Taking the probability of this event:
$$P(M \neq c) \le P\left(\bigcup_{j : p_j = 0} G_j\right) = \sum_{j : p_j = 0} p_j = 0$$

Thus, $P(M = c) = 1$ ($M = c$ almost surely). Conversely, if $P(M = c) = 1$, then $(M - c)^2 = 0$ outside a set of probability zero, yielding $\mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2] = 0$. $\blacksquare$

\sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})(X(\omega) - M(\omega))(M(\omega) - c) = (\mu_j - c) \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})(X(\omega) - \mu_j).
\]
Now consider the two cases for $p_j = P(G_j)$:

1. If $p_j = 0$, then $P(\{\omega\}) = 0$ for every $\omega \in G_j$ because $p_j = \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})$ is a sum of nonnegative probabilities. Every term in the sum over $G_j$ is zero, so the sum vanishes.
2. If $p_j > 0$, the definition of $\mu_j$ gives $\sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})X(\omega) = p_j \mu_j$. Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})(X(\omega) - \mu_j)
&= \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})X(\omega) - \mu_j \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\}) \\
&= p_j \mu_j - \mu_j p_j \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

In both cases the inner sum is zero, so each cell contributes zero:
\[
(\mu_j - c) \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})(X(\omega) - \mu_j) = 0.
\]
Summing over all $j = 1, \dots, m$ yields
\[
\mathbb{E}[(X - M)(M - c)] = \sum_{j=1}^m 0 = 0.
\]
Substituting this into the expanded square gives
\[
\mathbb{E}[(X - c)^2] = \mathbb{E}[(X - M)^2] + \mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2].
\]

Because $(M - c)^2 \ge 0$, its expectation is nonnegative:
\[
\mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2] \ge 0.
\]
Hence $\mathbb{E}[(X - c)^2] \ge \mathbb{E}[(X - M)^2]$. Equality holds if and only if $\mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2] = 0$. Partitioning that expectation gives
\[
\mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2] = \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{\omega \in G_j} P(\{\omega\})(\mu_j - c)^2 = \sum_{j=1}^m p_j (\mu_j - c)^2.
\]
Cells with $p_j = 0$ contribute zero to the expectation. For cells with $p_j > 0$, each term $p_j (\mu_j - c)^2$ is strictly positive unless $\mu_j = c$. Thus $\mathbb{E}[(M - c)^2] = 0$ if and only if $\mu_j = c$ for all $j$ with $p_j > 0$, which is the condition that $M = c$ with probability one.

### Claim

Arrange $n \ge 3$ distinctly labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots such that no two neighboring plots are selected, including the pair of plots that meet across the circular boundary. Then
$$A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.$$

---

### Proof

Throughout the argument, imagine the $n$ garden plots as having fixed, distinct labels $1, 2, \dots, n$ arranged in clockwise order around the circle, where plot $n$ and plot $1$ are neighbors across the circular boundary. Because the plots have fixed labels in the ground, two selections are the same if and only if they consist of the exact same set of plot labels; rotating a selection around the circle changes the labels of the chosen plots and therefore produces a different selection. Also note that because $n \ge 3$ and $k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, we always have $n - k \ge \lceil n/2 \rceil > 0$, so the denominator $n - k$ in the target formula is never zero.

---

#### Stage 1: The Empty Selection ($k = 0$)

We handle the case $k = 0$ separately because our main argument for $k \ge 1$ will mark one selected plot in each selection and later divide by $k$, neither of which is possible when no plots are selected.

* **What is being counted:** We are counting $0$-element subsets of the $n$ circular plots that contain no pair of adjacent plots.
* **Combinatorial count:** There is only one $0$-element subset—the empty selection $\emptyset$—and because it contains no plots at all, it vacuously contains no pair of neighboring plots. Thus, $A(n,0) = 1$.
* **Formula check:** Substituting $k = 0$ into the formula gives
  $$\frac{n}{n-0}\binom{n-0}{0} = \frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0} = 1 \cdot 1 = 1,$$
  since there is $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ way to choose $0$ objects from $n$ objects. Thus the formula holds for $k = 0$.

---

#### Stage 2: Double-Counting Marked Selections ($1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$)

Assume from now on that $1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. A circle has no natural first position, which makes it awkward to scan a selection from "left to right." To break this circular symmetry, we count **marked selections**.

* **What is being counted:** Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the set of all ordered pairs $(S, s_1)$, where:
  1. $S$ is a valid $k$-element selection of non-adjacent plots around the circle, and
  2. $s_1 \in S$ is one of the $k$ selected plots in $S$, chosen to carry a special marker as the "starting plot."

We now count the elements of $\mathcal{M}$ in two different ways.

##### Count 1: Grouping by the Unmarked Selection $S$
1. **Choose a valid unmarked selection $S$:** By definition, there are $A(n,k)$ valid $k$-element selections of non-adjacent plots around the circle.
2. **Mark a starting plot $s_1 \in S$:** Since $S$ consists of $k$ distinctly labeled plots, there are exactly $k$ choices for which plot in $S$ receives the start marker.

Each valid selection $S$ therefore generates exactly $k$ distinct marked selections $(S, s_1)$, and no two different selections $S \neq S'$ can produce the same pair $(S, s_1)$. Thus, the total number of marked selections is
$$|\mathcal{M}| = k \, A(n,k).$$

---

##### Count 2: Constructing a Marked Selection from a Start Label and Clockwise Gaps
Instead of choosing all $k$ plots at once, we can uniquely specify a marked selection $(S, s_1)$ by first choosing the location of the starting plot $s_1$ and then recording how many unselected plots we skip between consecutive selected plots as we walk clockwise around the circle.

1. **Choose the starting plot label $s_1$:**
   * *What is being counted:* The label of the marked starting plot $s_1$ among the $n$ fixed plots on the circle.
   * *Count:* Any of the $n$ plots can be chosen as $s_1$, giving $n$ possibilities.

2. **Translate the remaining configuration into an ordered tuple of gap sizes:**
   * *What is being counted:* Given a marked selection $(S, s_1)$, start at $s_1$ and walk clockwise around the circle, listing the $k$ selected plots in the order they are encountered: $s_1, s_2, \dots, s_k$. For each $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$, let $g_i$ be the number of **unselected** plots lying strictly between selected plot $s_i$ and the next selected plot $s_{i+1}$ in clockwise order, where $s_{k+1}$ means wrapping back around the circle to $s_1$. (In the case $k = 1$, there is only one selected plot $s_1$, and the single gap $g_1$ counts all $n - 1$ unselected plots encountered as we travel clockwise from $s_1$ all the way around the circle back to $s_1$.)
   * *Properties of the gap tuple $(g_1, g_2, \dots, g_k)$:*
     * Each $g_i$ is a positive integer ($g_i \ge 1$) because no two selected plots—including $s_k$ and $s_1$ across the wrap-around—are allowed to be adjacent on the circle; at least one unselected plot must separate them.
     * The sum of the gaps is $g_1 + g_2 + \dots + g_k = n - k$, because every plot on the circle is either one of the $k$ selected plots or one of the $n - k$ unselected plots, and each unselected plot belongs to exactly one clockwise gap.

3. **Count the valid gap tuples $(g_1, g_2, \dots, g_k)$:**
   * *What is being counted:* Ordered $k$-tuples of positive integers $(g_1, g_2, \dots, g_k)$ whose sum is $n - k$.
   * *Why the count is $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ (Stars-and-Bars with Positive Parts):*
     Imagine placing the $n - k$ unselected plots in a single row of $n - k$ dots:
     $$\bullet \;\; \bullet \;\; \bullet \;\; \cdots \;\; \bullet$$
     Between consecutive dots in this row of $n - k$ dots, there are $(n - k) - 1 = n - k - 1$ internal spaces. To divide the row of $n - k$ dots into $k$ consecutive, non-empty groups of sizes $g_1, g_2, \dots, g_k$ from left to right, we insert $k - 1$ separator bars into those $n - k - 1$ internal spaces—at most one bar per space, and none outside the ends of the row—so that every group contains at least one dot ($g_i \ge 1$).
     Thus, choosing an ordered tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers summing to $n - k$ is equivalent to choosing which $k - 1$ of the $n - k - 1$ internal spaces receive a separator bar. By the definition of the binomial coefficient (the number of ways to choose a $(k-1)$-element subset from a set of $n - k - 1$ elements), there are
     $$\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$$
     such tuples.
     *(Boundary check: When $k = 1$, we place $k - 1 = 0$ separators among $n - 2$ spaces, giving $\binom{n-2}{0} = 1$ tuple, namely $(n-1)$. At the upper extreme $k = n/2$ when $n$ is even, there are $n - k - 1 = k - 1$ internal spaces and we must place a separator in every single space, giving $\binom{k-1}{k-1} = 1$ tuple, namely $(1, 1, \dots, 1)$, where every gap has size $1$ and selected plots alternate with unselected plots around the circle.)*

4. **Verify the one-to-one correspondence (bijection):**
   * Every marked selection $(S, s_1)$ determines a unique start label $s_1$ and a unique clockwise gap tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$.
   * Conversely, any choice of start plot $s_1$ (from $n$ possibilities) and any tuple $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of positive integers summing to $n - k$ reconstructs a unique marked selection $(S, s_1)$: place the first marked plot at $s_1$, skip $g_1$ plots clockwise and select the next plot $s_2$, skip $g_2$ plots clockwise and select $s_3$, and so on up to $s_k$. Because the total number of clockwise steps around the circle is
     $$(g_1 + 1) + (g_2 + 1) + \dots + (g_k + 1) = (g_1 + \dots + g_k) + k = (n - k) + k = n,$$
     skipping $g_k$ unselected plots clockwise after $s_k$ lands back on $s_1$ after one exact revolution around the circle. Since every $g_i \ge 1$, no two consecutive selected plots (including $s_k$ and $s_1$) are adjacent.

Multiplying the $n$ choices for the start plot $s_1$ by the $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ independent choices for the clockwise gap tuple gives the second count of $\mathcal{M}$:
$$|\mathcal{M}| = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$

---

#### Stage 3: Dividing and Rewriting the Binomial Coefficient

Equating our two counts for $|\mathcal{M}|$ yields
$$k \, A(n,k) = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$

##### Why the Divisions are Legitimate
1. **Dividing by $k$:**
   * *Algebraically:* Because we handled $k = 0$ separately in Stage 1, we have $k \ge 1$, so $k \neq 0$.
   * *Combinatorially:* When we formed $\mathcal{M}$, we did not overcount different selections $S$ at different rates. Because the $n$ plots have distinct fixed labels, every valid $k$-element selection $S$ has exactly $k$ distinct plots that can be marked as $s_1$. Hence the map $(S, s_1) \mapsto S$ is an exact $k$-to-$1$ correspondence, guaranteeing that $n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ is divisible by $k$ and that the quotient
     $$A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$$
     is the exact integer count of unmarked valid selections. (Notice again that there is no division by $n$ for circular rotations because the plot labels are fixed in place; each rotation that moves the selected set of labels produces a genuinely different selection.)
2. **Dividing and multiplying by $n - k$ in the factorial identity:**
   Recall that for integers $0 \le r \le m$, the number of $r$-element subsets of an $m$-element set is given by the factorial formula $\binom{m}{r} = \frac{m!}{r!(m-r)!}$. Since $1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, we have $0 \le k - 1 \le n - k - 1$, $n - 2k \ge 0$, and $n - k > 0$. Expanding the binomial coefficient into factorials gives:
   $$\begin{aligned}
   A(n,k) &= \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1} \\
   &= \frac{n}{k} \cdot \frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,((n-k-1)-(k-1))!} \\
   &= \frac{n}{k} \cdot \frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}.
   \end{aligned}$$
   Using the factorial property $k \cdot (k-1)! = k!$ in the denominator, and multiplying both numerator and denominator by the non-zero integer $n - k$ so that $(n-k)\cdot(n-k-1)! = (n-k)!$, we obtain:
   $$\begin{aligned}
   A(n,k) &= \frac{n}{n-k} \cdot \frac{(n-k)(n-k-1)!}{k(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!} \\
   &= \frac{n}{n-k} \cdot \frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,((n-k)-k)!} \\
   &= \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
   \end{aligned}$$

This completes the proof for all $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. $\blacksquare$

### Theorem (Kaplansky’s Circular Lemma)
Let $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots be arranged clockwise in a circle, labeled $1, 2, \dots, n$, so that plot $i$ is adjacent to plot $i+1$ for $1 \le i \le n-1$, and plot $n$ is adjacent to plot $1$ across the circular boundary. 

For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n, k)$ denote the number of $k$-element subsets of plots such that no two chosen plots are adjacent along the circle. Then:
$$A(n, k) = \frac{n}{n-k} \binom{n-k}{k}$$

---

### Proof

#### 1. The Boundary Case: The Empty Selection ($k = 0$)
We first consider the case $k = 0$:
* **Combinatorial Count:** We are selecting $0$ plots from the $n$ available plots. There is exactly one such subset: the empty set $\emptyset$. The condition that "no two selected plots are neighbors" is vacuously satisfied because the selection contains no pairs of plots at all. Therefore:
  $$A(n, 0) = 1$$
* **Formula Verification:** Evaluating the proposed formula at $k = 0$:
  $$\frac{n}{n-0} \binom{n-0}{0} = \frac{n}{n} \cdot \binom{n}{0} = 1 \cdot 1 = 1$$
  Since $n \ge 3$, the denominator $n - 0 = n$ is strictly positive (no division by zero). The formula holds for $k = 0$.

For the remainder of the proof, we assume $k \ge 1$.

---

#### 2. The Auxiliary Set: "Marked" Valid Selections
To count the valid selections without getting trapped by circular symmetries, we define an auxiliary set of configurations:
$$\mathcal{M} = \{ (S, p) : S \text{ is a valid non-consecutive } k\text{-element selection, and } p \in S \}$$
An element of $\mathcal{M}$ is a valid selection $S$ with one of its chosen plots designated as a **marked start plot** $p$.

We count the size of $\mathcal{M}$ in two different ways.

---

#### 3. Method 1: Counting by Selections (Fiber Count)
* There are, by definition, $A(n, k)$ valid subsets $S$.
* For any chosen valid subset $S$, there are exactly $k$ plots in $S$. Any of these $k$ plots may be chosen as the marked start plot $p$.
* Because each valid selection contains the exact same number of plots ($k$), each selection $S$ generates exactly $k$ distinct pairs $(S, p) \in \mathcal{M}$.

Summing over all valid selections $S$, the total number of marked selections is:
$$|\mathcal{M}| = k \cdot A(n, k)$$

---

#### 4. Method 2: Counting by Starting Plot and Clockwise Gaps
Now we construct the pairs $(S, p) \in \mathcal{M}$ constructively from scratch:

1. **Choose the start plot $p$:**
   Since the plots have distinct, fixed labels $1, 2, \dots, n$, there are exactly $n$ possible choices for which labeled plot serves as the marked start plot $p_1 = p$.

2. **Traverse the circle clockwise:**
   Starting from $p_1$, list the remaining selected plots in clockwise order: $p_2, p_3, \dots, p_k$. 
   Let $g_i$ denote the number of unselected plots encountered strictly between selected plot $p_i$ and the next selected plot $p_{i+1}$ along the circle (for $1 \le i \le k$, with indices wrapping around so that $p_{k+1} = p_1$).

3. **Determine the conditions on the gap sizes $(g_1, g_2, \dots, g_k)$:**
   * **Non-adjacency:** No two selected plots may be adjacent. This means there must be at least one unselected plot between any two consecutive selected plots. Hence, each gap size must be a strictly positive integer:
     $$g_i \ge 1 \quad \text{for all } i \in \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$$
     *(Note: Because $g_k \ge 1$, the last selected plot $p_k$ cannot be adjacent to the starting plot $p_1$, correctly enforcing the circular boundary condition.)*
   * **Total unselected plots:** The selection contains $k$ plots out of $n$ total plots, leaving exactly $n - k$ plots unselected. Because every unselected plot lies in exactly one gap between consecutive selected plots:
     $$g_1 + g_2 + \cdots + g_k = n - k$$

4. **Count the gap distributions via first principles (Stars and Bars):**
   We need the number of ordered tuples of positive integers $(g_1, \dots, g_k)$ that sum to $n - k$.
   * Lay out the $n - k$ unselected plots in a line:
     $$\underbrace{\bullet \quad \bullet \quad \bullet \quad \dots \quad \bullet}_{n - k \text{ plots}}$$
   * Between these $n - k$ plots, there are exactly $(n - k) - 1$ interior spaces.
   * To split these $n - k$ items into $k$ non-empty contiguous groups ($g_1, g_2, \dots, g_k \ge 1$), we must place $k - 1$ identical dividing separators into these interior spaces, placing at most one separator per space.
   * The number of ways to choose $k - 1$ spaces out of the $(n - k - 1)$ available spaces is:
     $$\binom{n - k - 1}{k - 1}$$

Because the choice of start plot $p$ ($n$ possibilities) and the choice of clockwise gaps $\binom{n - k - 1}{k - 1}$ uniquely determine the marked selection $(S, p)$, and conversely every marked selection uniquely produces a start plot and a gap tuple, the total size of $\mathcal{M}$ is:
$$|\mathcal{M}| = n \binom{n - k - 1}{k - 1}$$

---

#### 5. Equating the Counts and Justifying Division
Equating the two counts of $|\mathcal{M}|$:
$$k \cdot A(n, k) = n \binom{n - k - 1}{k - 1}$$

##### Why division by $k$ is legitimate:
* **Non-zero divisor:** We assumed $k \ge 1$, so $k \ne 0$.
* **Uniform fiber size:** The map $(S, p) \mapsto S$ forgets the mark. Every valid selection $S$ has identical size $k$, meaning the preimage of any $S$ consists of precisely $k$ pairs. Dividing the total count of pairs by $k$ groups them into disjoint, equal-sized equivalence classes of size $k$, without fractional remainders or overcounting.

Thus:
$$A(n, k) = \frac{n}{k} \binom{n - k - 1}{k - 1}$$

---

#### 6. Algebraic Transformation to the Target Formula
To express $A(n, k)$ in the standard form $\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}$, we expand into factorials:

$$\binom{n - k - 1}{k - 1} = \frac{(n - k - 1)!}{(k - 1)! \, ((n - k - 1) - (k - 1))!} = \frac{(n - k - 1)!}{(k - 1)! \, (n - 2k)!}$$

Multiplying by $\frac{n}{k}$:
$$\frac{n}{k} \binom{n - k - 1}{k - 1} = \frac{n \cdot (n - k - 1)!}{[k \cdot (k - 1)!] \cdot (n - 2k)!} = \frac{n \cdot (n - k - 1)!}{k! \, (n - 2k)!}$$

Now multiply the numerator and the denominator by $(n - k)$:
$$= \frac{n \cdot (n - k) \cdot (n - k - 1)!}{(n - k) \cdot k! \, (n - 2k)!} = \frac{n}{n - k} \cdot \frac{(n - k)!}{k! \, ((n - k) - k)!} = \frac{n}{n - k} \binom{n - k}{k}$$

##### Why division by $n - k$ is legitimate:
Since $k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor \le n/2$, and $n \ge 3$:
$$n - k \ge n - \frac{n}{2} = \frac{n}{2} \ge \frac{3}{2} > 0$$
Thus, $n - k$ is strictly positive, so multiplying and dividing by $(n - k)$ does not divide by zero.

Combining this with the $k = 0$ base case completes the proof. $\blacksquare$

**Claim.** Let $P$ be a real $d \times d$ matrix with $P^2 = P$ and $P^T = P$, where $d \ge 1$. Let
\[
S = \{Pz : z \in \mathbb{R}^d\}
\]
be the set of permitted layout displacements, and define the squared Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{R}^d$ by $\|v\|^2 = v^T v$. For every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the unique $y \in S$ minimizing $\|x - y\|^2$ is $Px$. More precisely, for all $y \in S$,
\[
\|x - y\|^2 = \|x - Px\|^2 + \|Px - y\|^2.
\]

**Proof.** Fix $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and let $y \in S$. By the definition of $S$, the vector $Px$ belongs to $S$ (taking $z = x$), and there is some $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that $y = Pz$.

First, use the idempotence hypothesis $P^2 = P$ to evaluate $P$ on $Px$, on $y$, and on the residual $x - Px$. Multiplying by $P$ gives
\[
P(Px) = P^2 x = Px, \qquad Py = P(Pz) = P^2 z = Pz = y.
\]
By distributivity of matrix multiplication over subtraction, $P$ fixes $Px - y$ and maps $x - Px$ to the zero vector:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(Px - y) &= P(Px) - Py = Px - y,\\
P(x - Px) &= Px - P^2 x = Px - Px = 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Next, compute the inner product of $x - Px$ and $Px - y$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x - Px)^T(Px - y)
&= (x - Px)^T P(Px - y) && \text{(since } P(Px - y) = Px - y\text{)}\\
&= (x - Px)^T P^T(Px - y) && \text{(by symmetry, } P^T = P\text{)}\\
&= \bigl(P(x - Px)\bigr)^T(Px - y) && \text{(since } (AB)^T = B^T A^T\text{)}\\
&= 0^T(Px - y) && \text{(since } P(x - Px) = 0\text{)}\\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the transpose of the scalar $(x - Px)^T(Px - y) = 0$ also gives $(Px - y)^T(x - Px) = 0$.

Now split $x - y$ by subtracting and adding $Px$:
\[
x - y = (x - Px) + (Px - y).
\]
Using the definition $\|v\|^2 = v^T v$ and expanding the product by distributivity gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|x - y\|^2
&= \bigl((x - Px) + (Px - y)\bigr)^T\bigl((x - Px) + (Px - y)\bigr)\\

&= \|x - Px\|^2 + 0 + 0 + \|Px - y\|^2\\
&= \|x - Px\|^2 + \|Px - y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

In this decomposition, the first term $\|x - Px\|^2$ does not depend on $y$. The second term $\|Px - y\|^2 = (Px - y)^T(Px - y)$ is a sum of squares of real entries, so $\|Px - y\|^2 \ge 0$ for every $y \in S$, with equality if and only if $Px - y = 0$. Consequently, for all $y \in S$,
\[

\]

Thus $Px$ is the unique minimizer in $S$.
